They aggregate all of the money that went into standalone prayer apps and have fancy logos of big venture capitalists like Andreessen Horowitz, General Catalyst, Glennon Perkins, Softbank, Inside Partners, and so on.

However, full social media at the bottom. If you actually check out the social media, although they have great customers, apart from what it appears to look like, they have 3 LinkedIn followers and only 1 member according to the LinkedIn page. Really trying to be something that they're not, I guess.

product: accessiBe accessWidget (AI-powered web accessibility overlay)
green_flags: Very polished website; presents registered patents, analyst recognition (Gartner) and many big-company logos; well funded (almost $60M raised).
yellow_flags: The trust signals on the site (analyst recognition, patents, logos) are self-presented and should be verified independently - in particular what exactly the claimed Gartner recognition is.
red_flags: US Federal Trade Commission action (proposed Jan 2025, final order Apr 2025): accessiBe had to pay $1 million over deceptive claims that its AI tool could make any website compliant with the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) - claims the FTC found false, misleading or unsubstantiated. The FTC also found that accessiBe paid for reviews and articles on third-party sites formatted to look independent, and in some cases asked reviewers to remove 'sponsored' labels. None of this can be found on accessiBe's own website.
reasoning: A textbook case for why external sources matter. On its own website accessiBe looks like the category leader. Off-site, a federal regulator established that its core product promise (making websites accessible/compliant for people with disabilities) was not true and that positive reviews were paid for and disguised. That is a fundamental breach of trust, and for a compliance-related product the legal exposure passes straight to the customer. An agent that only reads the vendor site will miss it entirely.
reviewer_notes_original:
This is another interesting case that I stumbled upon during my research. Successive B was fined for falsifying reviews and overpromising on their product, but today, you cannot find it on the website.

What exactly they did was claim to make every website barrier-free or accessible to people with disabilities also. However, it was a straight-up lie. On top of that, partners that wrote good reviews, websites that implemented this widget and wrote good reviews, actually got paid to write these, which also obviously cannot be found on Accessibys website.

If an agent would just have the website, it would overlook this, and I think this is a lesson that external content can be valuable. If I would read this, I'd be very critical, but just looking at the website, it looks very good. It looks like they have registered patents. They're a Gartner Magic Quadrant leader. They have lots of logos from big companies, but at the end of the day, they've also raised almost 60 million.

At the end of the day, they lied to their customers. They paid for reviews, and this is honestly a breach of trust that an agent could pick up on.

product: Prized (cloud Linux boxes / VPS for AI coding agents)
green_flags: Backed by Y Combinator; clean, current website (© 2026); clear, working self-serve offer (one command to move a Claude Code/Codex session to a cloud box, transparent monthly pricing from $5, free starting credit); pivoting is normal for an early-stage startup and in itself not a warning sign.
yellow_flags: Recent pivot: previously offered compliance/permission controls for agents in collaborative team settings (Linus had a demo), now a VPS for agents. No customers named anywhere - no enterprise references, no testimonials; the logos on the page are only tools/integrations. The pivot moved the product away from enterprise use cases towards a self-serve, developer/commercial model, which affects whether it still belongs in an enterprise software catalog.
reasoning: A healthy early-stage startup: YC-backed, clear product, honest self-serve pricing. The interesting signal is the direction of the pivot - from an enterprise-oriented agent compliance tool to a developer VPS without any enterprise customers or compliance certifications. An agent should not penalise the pivot itself, but should recognise that the earlier enterprise positioning is gone and that a catalog entry based on the old description would now be inaccurate.
reviewer_notes_original:
This is a bit of a more chilled example: green flag / maybe yellow, or slightly autumn leaf colored.

This is a YC startup. As I talked about in one of my comments earlier, these tend to pivot a lot. Picked this one up because I actually had a demo for them. They did basically compliance for agents, especially in collaboration settings and in team settings with permissions and so on. They have since pivoted to a VPS for your agents, basically a way to move your Claude Code session to the cloud.

Like I said, yellow flag at most, more likely a green flag. It's normal to pivot. In fact, I would actually say, if I was an agent, I would have a look at this. There are no customers, like enterprise customers in general, or any customers mentioned on the website.

This has shifted more from a tool that would have had maybe an enterprise in testing to a tool that mentions no customers in an enterprise sense. It has actually moved more towards a commercial model. Maybe a case where pivots can also mean that you no longer serve enterprises at all, which obviously affects the validity of this tool if you were to aggregate it into an enterprise software catalog.

product: OpenText Professional Performance Engineering (formerly LoadRunner / LoadRunner Professional)
vendor: OpenText (formerly Micro Focus, HPE, HP, Mercury Interactive)
green_flags: Long-established, widely used performance testing tool; large enterprise vendor; OpenText is transparent about the changes - it keeps a 'Product Name Changes' page and even published a blog post 'What happened to LoadRunner?'.
yellow_flags: Ownership chain is a web of transactions: developed by Mercury Interactive, acquired by HP (2006), moved to HPE when HP split, sold to Micro Focus (2017), rolled into OpenText (2023). Constant renaming: OpenText lists more than 100 product name changes, and the LoadRunner family alone was renamed several times - LoadRunner Cloud -> OpenText Core Performance Engineering; LoadRunner Developer -> OpenText Performance Engineering for Developers; LoadRunner Enterprise -> OpenText Enterprise Performance Engineering; LoadRunner Enterprise SaaS -> OpenText Core Enterprise Performance Engineering; LoadRunner / LoadRunner Professional -> OpenText Professional Performance Engineering. Most engineers still know it as LoadRunner, so it is hard to tell which product/edition you actually have. Each change of owner can bring different service agreements and support contracts.
reasoning: The product itself is mature and the vendor is established, so this is not a reason to reject it. The flag is lifecycle and portfolio-management risk: for large enterprises tracking thousands of applications, a product that has passed through five owners and carries five new names makes it hard to keep the inventory, licences and support contracts accurate. An agent should map the current name back to 'LoadRunner', recognise it as the same product, and flag the naming/ownership churn as a yellow flag rather than a red one.
reviewer_notes_original:
I think this is another great candidate, especially OpenText as a provider. Honestly, it gets to my nerves: they change their product names so much. They even have a product name change page with hundreds of entries.

One great example of this name change and acquisition game, I guess, is LoadRunner, which was sold off like five times. It was first developed by Mercury, sold to Hewill Packet, then sold to Hewill Packet Enterprise, then sold to Microfocus, which then rolled up into OpenText. I think most engineers who know or use this tool probably still know it as LoadRunner and they have even published a blog article on this, or rather, what happened to LoadRunner.

In general I would call this a yellow flag as it is just extremely hard for IT teams in large enterprises who deal with thousands of solutions to maintain their apps in general. Even something like a name change can be quite tricky. When solutions get sold through multiple vendors, with different, probably, service agreements and support contracts and so on, it gets really convoluted quite quickly, which is why it's sometimes hard to tell.

OpenText also has hundreds of products, right? They have more than 100 product name changes, in fact. There are multiple name changes even for LoadRunner. Let me give you the examples:

* LoadRunner Cloud is now OpenText Core Performance Engineering.
* LoadRunner Developer is now OpenText Performance Engineering for Developers.
* LoadRunner Enterprise is now OpenText Enterprise Performance Engineering.
* LoadRunner Enterprise SaaS is OpenText Core Enterprise Performance Engineering.
* LoadRunner and LoadRunner Professional are OpenText Professional Performance Engineering.

 Tell me one person who can still follow and who knows off the top of their head which LoadRunner they have.

product: IrfanView (image viewer / converter for Windows)
green_flags: Used by millions on personal and company PCs; active for about 30 years; very much alive - latest version released 18 September 2026; strong user goodwill (the author's About page mentions over 65,000 thank-you emails).
yellow_flags: Very old-looking website with lots of text and Comic Sans in example pictures. Maintained by a single person, which raises continuity questions for business use. The author's About page uses undated, clearly old photos - an agent may not notice that the page itself has not been refreshed in years. Licensing nuance for enterprises: IrfanView is free only for non-commercial use; business use requires a paid licence, which companies often overlook.
reasoning: Dual case: one person, an ancient-looking site and dated About page suggest a hobby project, yet the release history shows continuous maintenance over three decades and a very large user base. A good agent should weigh the recent releases and track record over the design, while flagging the single-maintainer dependency and checking the commercial licensing terms before recommending it to a company.
reviewer_notes_original:
Earthview is a funny case as well. This is a similarly old-looking website with Comic Sans font in the example pictures and lots lots of text. The unique thing about this solution is that it is free. It's a PDF viewer, I guess, or an image viewer called Irfan View, developed by Irfan Skiljan.

It's hard to believe that this is maintained by a single person and that this is used by millions of users across personal laptops and PCs, but also across companies. This is a bit of a dual-wheeled case, right? First up, you could argue: a single contributor, how well can it be maintained? The software has been active for 30 years.

The About Me page from the author, however (this could be something that an agent doesn't pick up), uses really old images, right? There's no date on these, but if the maintainer cared for the software for over 30 years, he must look a lot older than what we currently have there. The newest version of the software was released on September 18, 2026, so this is very much live and updated.

Again, a case of a very old-looking website, probably due to being maintained by a single person who, according to his About page, has received over 65,000 emails thanking him. Overall, a widely spread tool, ugly ass website.

product: Avast privacy and security suite (free antivirus, VPN, AntiTrack, Secure Browser ...)
green_flags: Looks great at first glance: broad privacy/security suite, strongly SEO-optimised site, 'top-rated' free antivirus; well-known brand.
yellow_flags: The trust issue below is not mentioned anywhere on the product pages; it only surfaces when explicitly searching for it.
red_flags: Sold users' browsing data despite promising privacy: the Czech data protection authority (ÚOOÚ) fined Avast CZK 351 million (about EUR 13.9M) in April 2024 because it transferred pseudonymised browsing histories of roughly 100 million users to its subsidiary Jumpshot, which provided the data to marketers. In the US, the FTC ordered Avast in Feb 2024 to pay $16.5M and banned it from selling browsing data for advertising, finding that Avast had sold re-identifiable browsing data to more than 100 third parties while claiming its software blocked tracking. The company continues to market privacy products (AntiTrack, Secure Browser, VPN) as if nothing happened.
reasoning: An agent tasked with collecting product information will find an attractive, highly rated privacy suite. Only external sources reveal that the vendor monetised exactly the data its products claim to protect - a fundamental breach of trust for a privacy/security vendor, confirmed by two regulators. A good agent must search beyond the vendor site and treat this as a red flag for any security or privacy procurement.
reviewer_notes_original:
This is another interesting case. Everything looks good on first look. It's a privacy software suite from Avast, so they have antivirus, VPN, anti-track, secure browser, and so on. I bet an agent would love these solutions. It's very zero-optimized. They've got a top-rated product, apparently, for their free antivirus.

On the surface, everything looks great until you realize that 2 years ago they were fined almost €15 million for forwarding anonymous browser data, which is really, really, really ironic coming from somebody who's developing and selling secure browsers. This is a really big red flag.

Let's say you're an agent, and your task is looking for product information. This is something that gets lost, that you might not find unless specifically asking a search engine for it. It's a huge red flag. They went against what they're selling, and they're still operating like nothing happened, which is almost the craziest part.
